books.section: American Involvement in Vietnam, World War II–1963

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from the grounding books' account of the Tet Offensive

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Tet Offensive, January 1968, from the grounding books.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the Tet Offensive, January 1968. During the Tet holiday truce, Vietcong and North Vietnamese forces attacked cities and bases across South Vietnam, including Saigon and Hue. American and South Vietnamese forces drove them back with heavy losses: more than 40,000 North Vietnamese and Vietcong dead, against about 1,600 Americans dead. Yet the scale of the attack shocked Americans at home, who had been told victory was near.

stem: The Tet Offensive is best understood as a military defeat for the Communists that was also a political victory for them because it did which of the following?

options.text: It captured Saigon and forced the United States to surrender at once
options.misconception: The Communists did not capture Saigon or force a surrender; American and South Vietnamese forces drove them back.

options.text: It showed Americans the enemy could strike anywhere, shaking trust that victory was near
It ended all fighting in Vietnam for the rest of the war years
options.misconception: Background: fighting continued for years after Tet; the war did not end in 1968.

options.text: It proved that North Vietnam had no army left to fight with
options.misconception: Background: the Communists lost heavily but kept fighting for years, so they still had an army.

rationales.A: The passage says American and South Vietnamese forces drove the attackers back, so Saigon was not captured.
rationales.B: Background: the attack struck cities across South Vietnam, and its scale shocked Americans who had been told victory was near.
rationales.C: Background: the war continued for years after Tet, until 1973 for American forces and 1975 for Saigon.
rationales.D: The passage says the Communists lost more than 40,000 dead. Background: they kept fighting, so their army was not gone.
rationales.general:
1. Count the losses in the passage: more than 40,000 North Vietnamese and Vietcong dead against about 1,600 Americans.
2. By the casualty count, the offensive was a heavy military defeat for the attackers.
3. Background: the attack still struck cities across South Vietnam during a holiday truce, which shocked Americans at home.
4. That shock matters because officials had told the public victory was near, and Tet made that claim hard to believe.
Remember: A battle can be lost on the field and still win the argument at home.
